title: Understanding the Cyber Threat Landscape
subtopics: Individual, Organized, and State-Sponsored Threat Actors
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Understanding the Cyber Threat Landscape.
Apply understanding the cyber threat landscape to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers understanding the cyber threat landscape in the Cyber Threats and Attack Fundamentals track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Treat attacker lifecycle models as analytical lenses, not a promise that every incident follows the same linear sequence. The specific focus here is understanding the cyber threat landscape; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Understanding the Cyber Threat Landscape focuses on cybercrime, espionage, and disruption; individual, organized, and state-sponsored threat actors; insider threats. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: Cybercrime, Espionage, and Disruption
items.text: For cybercrime, espionage, and disruption, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Individual, Organized, and State-Sponsored Threat Actors
items.text: A threat actor is a person or group whose goals, capabilities, resources, and opportunities shape the risk. Attribute behavior cautiously and distinguish observed evidence from speculation.

items.title: Insider Threats
items.text: For insider threats, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Opportunistic and Targeted Attacks
items.text: For opportunistic and targeted attacks, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Motives, Capabilities, and Opportunities
items.text: For motives, capabilities, and opportunities, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Threat Intelligence and Uncertainty
items.text: Threat intelligence is useful when it includes source, time, confidence, relevance, and a defensive action. Map observed behavior to current ATT&CK entries cautiously; a match is a hypothesis that needs corroborating evidence.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: Threat analysis links an actor's goal and opportunity to a possible path of harm, then looks for evidence and defensive interruption points. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Understanding the Cyber Threat Landscape focuses on cybercrime, espionage, and disruption; individual, organized, and state-sponsored threat actors; insider threats. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Understanding the Cyber Threat Landscape. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Cybercrime, Espionage, and Disruption; Individual, Organized, and State-Sponsored Threat Actors; Insider Threats), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.

demo-web-01 review: new_admin_role
troubleshooting: The example is illustrative and should be reviewed against current platform/version documentation before production use.
If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.
Use only fake data and remove all temporary local artifacts when the exercise is complete.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Understanding the Cyber Threat Landscape is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.

sources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.notes: CSF 2.0 defines outcome-oriented functions and does not prescribe one mandatory implementation. Verify the current CSF resources before publication.

sources.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1
sources.notes: CIS v8.1 aligns control mappings with NIST CSF 2.0. Select safeguards according to context, risk, and operating constraints.

sources.title: NICE Framework Resource Center
sources.notes: Use the current NICE Framework components when mapping knowledge and skills to work roles.

sources.title: Secure by Design
sources.notes: Use as a design-practice reference, not as a certification or proof that a product is secure.
